meta.description: Paintings influenced by, or critically connected to, Claude Monet's Water Lilies (Les Nymphéas). Intended as edge targets for a d3/React visualization whose source catalog is water_lilies_catalog.json. Monet painting IDs use the Wildenstein catalogue raisonné numbers (e.g. W.1973) present in water_lilies_catalog.json's `catalog_number` field; Orangerie panels use the 'First room: N' / 'Second room: N' keys from the same file.

connection_type_legend.all-over: Compositional evenness, no figure/ground hierarchy (Greenberg's Monet→Pollock argument).
connection_type_legend.horizonless: No anchoring horizon line; the pond-surface trick abstracted.
connection_type_legend.scale-immersive: Room-filling canvases that envelop the viewer (Grandes Décorations → Rothko Chapel, Newman).
connection_type_legend.color-field: Large expanses of modulated color doing the expressive work.
connection_type_legend.direct-homage: Artist explicitly quotes the Water Lilies motif.
connection_type_legend.biographical: Artist lived near Giverny / visited the pond / knew Monet's circle.
connection_type_legend.loose-critical: Typological or retrospective critical link only.

connection_strength_legend.direct: Artist said it (letters, interviews, studio statements).
connection_strength_legend.documented: Scholar or curator has proved it with archival evidence.
connection_strength_legend.critical: Critic or curator drew the link at the time or since.
connection_strength_legend.loose: Typological resemblance only; no documentary chain.

paintings.title: Autumn Rhythm (Number 30)
paintings.collection: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: Clement Greenberg's 1956 essay 'The Later Monet' argued that Pollock's all-over, horizonless webs continue the pictorial logic of Monet's late Water Lilies; Alfred Barr's acquisition and installation of Monet's triptych at MoMA (W.1973) was staged to make that lineage visible alongside Pollock.
paintings.citation: Clement Greenberg, 'The Later Monet,' Art News Annual 26 (1957), 132–148.

paintings.title: One: Number 31, 1950
paintings.medium: oil and enamel on unprimed canvas
paintings.collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: Greenberg described Pollock's 'vaporous dust of interfused lights' as reminding him of Monet's late style. One: Number 31 is the canonical Pollock housed at MoMA, exhibited yards from the Water Lilies triptych (W.1973) acquired the same year — a pairing Alfred Barr orchestrated to make the lineage explicit.
paintings.citation: Clement Greenberg, cited in New Criterion 'Floating on the Lilies,' 2018.

paintings.title: The Deep
paintings.connection_claim: Included in the Orangerie 2018 exhibition pairing Monet and Pollock, though The Art Newspaper argued the work is more indebted to Clyfford Still than Monet — the gash of white into dark ground reads as Still's vertical tear logic rather than Monet's submerged horizon.
paintings.citation: Brooklyn Rail, 'Water Lilies: American Abstract Painting and the Last Monet,' October 2018.
paintings._note: The Art Newspaper skeptical counter-reading argues Pollock's Deep is more indebted to Clyfford Still than Monet: https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2018/08/17/what-debt-does-mid-century-american-abstract-painting-owe-to-monet

paintings.title: No. 14, 1960
paintings.collection: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA)
paintings.connection_claim: Curators and critics from William Seitz (MoMA 1960) onward read Rothko's wall-scaled color envelopes as the post-war American analogue of the Orangerie's curved, room-sized immersion — the viewer is placed inside color rather than in front of an image.
paintings.citation: William C. Seitz, Monet: Seasons and Moments, exh. cat. (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1960).

paintings.title: Rothko Chapel, North Apse Triptych
paintings.medium: oil and mixed media on canvas
paintings.dimensions: central panel 457.2 × 304.8 cm; flanking panels each c. 335.3 × 243.8 cm
paintings.image_url_comment: Image rights strictly controlled by the Mark Rothko Foundation; no reproduction without license. See image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: The Rothko Chapel is routinely read as a non-denominational American descendant of the Orangerie's two oval rooms: a site-specific, purpose-built environment whose meaning is produced by wrapping the spectator in a continuous field of painted color.
paintings.citation: Robert Rosenblum, Modern Painting and the Northern Romantic Tradition: Friedrich to Rothko (Harper & Row, 1975), chapter 7.

paintings.title: No. 61 (Rust and Blue)
paintings.collection: Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles
paintings.image_url_comment: Held by MOCA Los Angeles; MOCA does not publish IIIF or an open image API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Rothko's dissolving rust-and-blue rectangles share Monet's horizonless field logic — floating colour zones that refuse ground. Greenberg framed both as heirs to an 'all-over' empirical sensuousness, though Rothko himself pointed to Bonnard as the more immediate trigger.
paintings.citation: Clement Greenberg, 'American-Type Painting,' Partisan Review 22:2 (1955); contested in Art Newspaper 2018.
paintings._note: Rothko Chapel (1971) carries the Orangerie oval-room immersive logic further; see rothko-chapel-north-triptych-1966.

paintings.title: Multiform
paintings.connection_claim: Included in the Orangerie 2018 exhibition. The Art Newspaper argues that Bonnard's 1948 MoMA retrospective — not Monet — was the direct trigger for these early multiforms dissolving figurative presences into glowing fields.
paintings.citation: Art Newspaper, 2018; Orangerie catalogue 2018.

paintings.title: Vir Heroicus Sublimis
paintings.collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: Newman's wall statement — 'The large pictures in this exhibition are intended to be seen from a short distance' — codifies the same immersive, peripheral-vision experience Monet engineered at the Orangerie: the canvas is a field the viewer stands inside, not a window.
paintings.citation: Barnett Newman, wall statement for his second exhibition at Betty Parsons Gallery, April 1951; reprinted in John P. O'Neill (ed.), Barnett Newman: Selected Writings and Interviews (Knopf, 1990), 178.

paintings.title: La Grande Vallée XIV (For a Little While)
paintings.image_url_comment: Centre Pompidou publishes no open IIIF image endpoint. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Mitchell lived from 1968 until her death in the house at Vétheuil on the hillside above Monet's earlier property; her late multi-panel landscapes were read by curators (most explicitly in the 2022 Fondation Louis Vuitton 'Monet–Mitchell' pairing) as a direct, lived continuation of Monet's Grandes Décorations.
paintings.citation: Suzanne Pagé and Angela Lampe (eds.), Monet–Mitchell, exh. cat. (Paris: Fondation Louis Vuitton / Hazan, 2022).

paintings.title: Mountains and Sea
paintings.medium: oil and charcoal on unprimed canvas
paintings.collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C. (Gift of the artist)
paintings.image_url_comment: NGA holds the work but the TMS API endpoint (api.nga.gov/art/tms) returned 404 — the endpoint has been deprecated. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Frankenthaler's soak-stain technique — pigment soaking into unprimed canvas so that image and support are one membrane — was read by Greenberg and Michael Fried as the American crystallisation of the optical indeterminacy of Monet's late pond paintings, where water, reflection, and painted surface collapse into a single field.
paintings.citation: Michael Fried, 'Morris Louis,' in Art and Objecthood (University of Chicago Press, 1998), 102–121; orig. 1967.

paintings.title: Tet
paintings.collection: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
paintings.image_url_comment: Whitney Museum publishes no open image API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: The Veil paintings' translucent overlaid washes were framed by Greenberg and later by John Elderfield as the most disciplined inheritance of Monet's submerged greens at the Orangerie: pigment is no longer on the canvas, it is the canvas, just as Monet's water had no surface.
paintings.citation: John Elderfield, Morris Louis, exh. cat. (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1986).

paintings.title: Towards Disappearance II
paintings.collection: Albright-Knox Art Gallery (now Buffalo AKG), Buffalo, New York
paintings.image_url_comment: Buffalo AKG publishes no open image API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Sam Francis, living in Paris through the 1950s and working at mural scale, repeatedly cited the Orangerie as the decisive modern precedent; Peter Selz framed his white-centred, edge-gathered compositions as Francis's version of Monet's pond — emptiness in the middle, colour-event at the periphery.
paintings.citation: Peter Selz, Sam Francis (New York: Harry N. Abrams, 1975; rev. ed. 1982).

paintings.title: Dial
paintings.collection: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: The term 'Abstract Impressionism' was coined by Louis Finkelstein in 1956 precisely to describe Guston's pulsing, centre-weighted dabs of pink, red and grey — paint behaving like the late Monet's chromatic haze, without Pollock's drawn linearity.
paintings.citation: Louis Finkelstein, 'New Look: Abstract-Impressionism,' ARTnews 55 (March 1956), 36–39, 66–68.

paintings.title: Untitled V
paintings.image_url_comment: De Kooning Foundation embargoes most commercial reproductions; no public image API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: De Kooning's late-1970s 'pastoral' paintings, made in East Hampton on canvases kept wet for weeks, were identified by curators including Diane Waldman and later Richard Shiff as his explicit attempt to regain Monet's watery, weather-soaked palette.
paintings.citation: Richard Shiff, Between Sense and de Kooning (Reaktion Books, 2011), 142–167.

paintings.title: Tableau Vert
paintings.image_url_comment: Ellsworth Kelly Foundation controls all reproduction rights; no public API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Kelly visited Giverny in 1952 and found Monet's then-dust-covered late panels in the abandoned Atelier des Nymphéas; Tableau Vert — a single modulated green rectangle — is documented by Kelly himself as a direct response to that encounter, painted within weeks of his visit.
paintings.citation: Yve-Alain Bois, Ellsworth Kelly: The Years in France, 1948–1954, exh. cat. (Washington, D.C.: National Gallery of Art, 1992).

paintings.title: Water Lilies with Japanese Bridge
paintings.medium: enamel on processed and swirled stainless steel
paintings.image_url_comment: Lichtenstein Foundation strictly licenses all reproductions; no public endpoint. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Lichtenstein's Water Lilies series of 1992 reproduces the Japanese Footbridge compositions in Ben-Day dots and stainless steel — an explicitly parodic homage that re-reads Monet's surface as already a printed, reproducible sign.
paintings.citation: Roy Lichtenstein, interview with Michael Kimmelman, The New York Times, October 9, 1992.

paintings.title: Quattro Stagioni: Primavera
paintings.medium: acrylic, oil, crayon and pencil on canvas
paintings.connection_claim: Twombly's Quattro Stagioni — seasonal cycles of dripped crimson, green and ochre — were framed by Richard Leeman and by Tate curators as late-modernist seasonal pendants to Monet's year-long pond observations: cycles of dissolution rather than landscapes.
paintings.citation: Richard Leeman, Cy Twombly: A Monograph (Thames & Hudson, 2005), 242–260.

paintings.title: Cold Mountain 6 (Bridge)
paintings.collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.
paintings.image_url_comment: NGA holds the work but the TMS API endpoint (api.nga.gov/art/tms) returned 404 — the endpoint has been deprecated. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Gary Garrels and Richard Shiff both described Marden's calligraphic, looping Cold Mountain paintings as a late-twentieth-century equivalent of Monet's late Japanese Footbridge canvases — an abstraction derived from arboreal, reflected line rather than from grid or geometry.
paintings.citation: Gary Garrels (ed.), Plane Image: A Brice Marden Retrospective, exh. cat. (New York: MoMA, 2006).

paintings.title: Genie
paintings.image_url_comment: Estate only; no public API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Resnick is the other painter named by Finkelstein in the 1956 'Abstract-Impressionism' essay; his late-1950s paintings are dense, edge-to-edge crusts of broken colour that critics repeatedly described as post-war Nymphéas in thicker paint.
paintings.citation: Louis Finkelstein, 'New Look: Abstract-Impressionism,' ARTnews 55 (March 1956), 36–39, 66–68.

paintings.title: PH-950 (1950-A No. 2)
paintings.image_url_comment: Clyfford Still Museum publishes no open image API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Still rejected European precedents and specifically refused the Monet comparison, but curators from Dean Sobel onward have noted typological proximity: wall-height, horizonless fields of modulated colour punctured by thin tears — the same bodily-scale proposition as the Orangerie.
paintings.citation: Dean Sobel and David Anfam, Clyfford Still: The Artist's Museum (Skira Rizzoli, 2012).

paintings.title: Seestück (See-See)
paintings.image_url_comment: gerhard-richter.com provides no image-download API; estate controls all reproductions. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Richter's Seestücke splice two photographs of water into a horizonless mirror; Dietmar Elger and Benjamin Buchloh both invoked late Monet as the obvious nineteenth-century precedent for a painting whose only subject is the optical impossibility of water meeting water.
paintings.citation: Dietmar Elger, Gerhard Richter: A Life in Painting (University of Chicago Press, 2009), 180–194.

paintings.title: Waterfall
paintings.image_url_comment: Pat Steir estate only; no public image API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Steir has repeatedly named Monet as a primary reference and credits the Orangerie with her decision to let gravity and dilution — not drawing — carry the image; her poured Waterfalls restage the late Nymphéas' subject (water falling through water) as process.
paintings.citation: Pat Steir, in conversation with Anne Waldman, BOMB Magazine 83 (Spring 2003).

paintings.title: Architecture of the Sky III
paintings.image_url_comment: Guggenheim Museum publishes no open image endpoint. Retrieve manually from image_source_page.
paintings.connection_claim: Bleckner's dark, dotted, light-pierced fields were read by Lisa Phillips as late-twentieth-century sky-versions of Monet's cloud-reflection panels at the Orangerie — the same device (suspended points of illumination on a dark chromatic ground) transposed from water to sky.
paintings.citation: Lisa Phillips, Ross Bleckner, exh. cat. (New York: Guggenheim Museum, 1995).

paintings.title: Earthly Paradise
paintings.connection_claim: Rothko explicitly named Bonnard as a key predecessor in dissolving figure into chromatic field; critics from Dore Ashton onward positioned Bonnard's garden paintings as the French bridge between Monet's chromatic dissolution and the American Color Field, with the decisive moment being the 1948 MoMA Bonnard retrospective — attended by both Rothko and de Kooning.
paintings.citation: Dore Ashton, About Rothko (Oxford University Press, 1983), 78–80; James Breslin, Mark Rothko: A Biography (University of Chicago Press, 1993), 246.

paintings.title: Leaf
paintings.image_url_comment: Image rights controlled by Agnes Martin Foundation; Tate does not publish open IIIF images for in-copyright works. Retrieve manually from image_source_page (Tate accession T01852).
paintings.connection_claim: Tate and MoMA curators link Martin's uninterrupted horizontal grids — which leave no hierarchy between top, middle, and bottom — to Monet's pond-surface paintings, where the canvas is entirely middle-distance with no foothold above or below. Ann Wilson Lloyd framed Martin's bands as the post-war analogue of Monet's dissolved horizon.
paintings.citation: Ann Wilson Lloyd, 'Agnes Martin and the Sublimity of Abstraction,' in Agnes Martin, exh. cat. (New York: Whitney Museum of American Art, 1992).

paintings.title: Spring
paintings.collection: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
paintings.image_url_comment: Image rights controlled by the Pollock-Krasner Foundation; Whitney publishes no open image API. Retrieve manually from image_source_page (Whitney accession 69.19).
paintings.connection_claim: One of the largest all-over AbEx paintings, Spring's mosaic of botanical fragments across 4.2 metres was framed by Barbara Rose and Ellen Landau in the context of Greenberg's Monet/AbEx lineage: scale, organic fragmentation, and the refusal of spatial hierarchy mirror Pollock's reading of Monet's late pond paintings.
paintings.citation: Ellen G. Landau, Lee Krasner: A Catalogue Raisonné (Abrams, 1995), cat. 159; Barbara Rose, Lee Krasner: A Retrospective, exh. cat. (MoMA/Houston, 1983).

paintings.title: Blue Monochrome (IKB 79)
paintings.medium: dry pigment in synthetic resin on gauze mounted on board
paintings.collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York
paintings.connection_claim: Klein's IKB monochromes were described by Klein himself as 'void' paintings — colour as pure space with no image — a proposition identical to Monet's Orangerie panels, where the surface offers no vantage point outside itself; Thomas McEvilley drew the explicit line in his 1982 MoMA Klein exhibition essay, framing IKB as a French post-war response to the environmental logic of the Grandes Décorations.
paintings.citation: Thomas McEvilley, 'Yves Klein: Conquistador of the Void,' in Yves Klein: A Retrospective, exh. cat. (Houston: Institute for the Arts, Rice University, 1982).
